headline: Orlando works the tourism machine and is tired of being its backdrop.
summary: Almost nobody in Orlando is from Orlando, so identity comes from neighborhoods, diaspora communities and a few shared symbols: the 407, the Magic, Lake Eola's swan, the City Beautiful. Locals are tired of being reduced to Disney, Universal and Florida jokes. Grief and resilience after the 2016 Pulse shooting run deep. The Shaq and Penny pinstripes supply the nostalgia, and Banchero and Wagner carry the present.

insights.title: The chip about the theme parks
insights.detail: Locals work the tourism economy as cast members, servers and housekeepers, and they resent being treated as backdrop. Pride lives in neighborhoods and the 407, not in park imagery.
insights.implication: Skip castles, mouse ears and park-style fantasy graphics. Lead with neighborhood names, area codes and local landmarks that read as insider.

insights.title: A city of transplants rallies around the Magic
insights.detail: With few multigenerational natives, the Magic, Orlando City and the Pride are the shared civic glue. The mythology is the 1995 and 2009 Finals runs and the Shaq, Penny, McGrady and Dwight eras. Pinstripes and the star-and-ball logo are still the most beloved Magic marks.
insights.implication: Heritage pinstripes and Hardaway-era references land harder than generic city graphics. Pair the legacy with Banchero and Wagner to bring old and new fans together.

insights.title: Puerto Rican and wider Caribbean Orlando
insights.detail: Central Florida has one of the largest Puerto Rican populations on the mainland, concentrated in east Orlando, Kissimmee and Osceola County. It grew after Hurricane Maria in 2017. Three Kings Day, coqui imagery, pastelillos and coquito are everyday markers.
insights.implication: A Boricua-rooted capsule can be strong. Partner with Puerto Rican designers, illustrators and community groups from Central Florida, and pay them. Don't lift symbols, and don't stop at a flag recolor.

insights.title: Parramore and Eatonville: Black heritage that predates the parks
insights.detail: Parramore is Orlando's historic Black neighborhood, next to the arena and home to the Wells'Built Museum. Highway construction and downtown development reshaped it. A few miles north, Eatonville is one of the country's earliest incorporated Black municipalities and Zora Neale Hurston's hometown.
insights.implication: Product that credits Hurston's legacy and Parramore voices can be powerful. Build it with community partners, and leave real benefit in the neighborhoods. It can't be decoration.

insights.title: Mills 50 and the Vietnamese and Asian corridor
insights.detail: Mills 50 and the East Colonial Drive corridor, sometimes called Little Saigon, hold Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean and other Asian businesses, murals and night markets, alongside indie music and coffee. It is the city's most creative, youth-driven pocket.
insights.implication: Neon signage, hand-painted storefront lettering and mural palettes are the real cues. Work with Mills 50 artists and merchants on any graphic.

insights.title: Resilience, and Pulse as a sacred subject
insights.detail: Since June 2016, Orlando's identity includes Orlando United and the onePULSE Foundation's memorial work. The LGBTQ+ community is also central, through Gay Days and Come Out With Pride.
insights.implication: Support Pride visibility with real community partners. Never commercialize the Pulse tragedy or its imagery on product.

insights.title: Climate: sun, storms and citrus-state color
insights.detail: Summer brings heat, humidity and near-daily afternoon thunderstorms, and hurricane season runs June through November. Locals dress light and bright, in breathable fabrics, shorts and sandals. The grove, lake and sunset palette is part of the self-image.
insights.implication: Prioritize lightweight, quick-dry, vented warm-ups and shooting shirts. Add rain-ready outerwear and sun-faded citrus and lake tones.

places.name: Kia Center
places.why: The Magic's home and the civic gathering point, beside historic Parramore.

places.name: Lake Eola Park
places.why: The swan boats and fountain are the best-known local postcard that isn't a theme park. The Sunday farmers market is a ritual.

places.name: Wells'Built Museum of African American History and Culture
places.why: A cornerstone of Black Orlando's history, in a building tied to the community's pre-integration life.

places.name: Mills 50 District
places.why: Vietnamese and pan-Asian food, murals and indie music. Locals claim it as their creative hub.

places.name: Thornton Park
places.why: Brick streets, cafes and neighborhood-scale identity, just east of Lake Eola.

places.name: Eatonville and the Zora Neale Hurston National Museum of Fine Arts
places.why: Hurston's hometown and a landmark of Black self-governance. It hosts the annual ZORA! Festival.

places.name: Orange Blossom Trail
places.why: The old highway through Black and Caribbean Orlando, with long local memory and street-level culture.

places.name: Park Avenue and Hannibal Square
places.why: Winter Park's historic main street, and next to it Hannibal Square, the historically Black neighborhood.

places.name: Dr. Phillips Center for the Performing Arts
places.why: The city's main stage for Broadway, concerts and arts, next door to Kia Center.

places.name: Orlando Museum of Art and Loch Haven Park
places.why: Anchor of the local arts campus near Mills 50, alongside Mennello and the science center.

people.name: Zora Neale Hurston
people.why: Raised in Eatonville, she is the literary symbol of Black Central Florida and the namesake of its biggest heritage festival.

people.name: Penny Hardaway
people.why: The face of the 1990s Magic and the pinstripe era. His signature Nike product is already part of Orlando memory.

people.name: Shaquille O'Neal
people.why: Orlando's first superstar and a 1995 Finals icon. His arrival put the franchise on the national map.

people.name: Tracy McGrady
people.why: The early 2000s scoring star, still a cult figure in Central Florida.

people.name: Dwight Howard
people.why: Led the team to the 2009 Finals and still anchors local memory of that run.

people.name: Nick Anderson
people.why: A franchise original and a face of the 1995 team.

people.name: Paolo Banchero
people.why: The current franchise face, an Orlando-first star the city rallies behind.

people.name: Franz Wagner
people.why: Co-star of the young core, a favorite with national and local fans alike.

moments.name: 407 Day
moments.why: The informal local holiday for the area code, and a natural moment for city-pride product.

moments.name: ZORA! Festival
moments.why: Eatonville's celebration of Hurston and Black arts, and the main heritage moment for Black Orlando.

moments.name: Three Kings Day
moments.why: A major Puerto Rican and Latino tradition in Central Florida.

moments.name: Hispanic Heritage Month
moments.why: Lines up with the start of the NBA season and with Magic Latino-themed nights.

moments.name: Gay Days
moments.why: A decades-old LGBTQ+ gathering in Orlando, now overlapping the NBA Finals period.

moments.name: Pulse remembrance
moments.why: A solemn community anniversary. Respect it, and don't use it to sell.

moments.name: Come Out With Pride
moments.why: Orlando's annual Pride celebration, close to the Magic's home opener.

moments.name: Magic home games at Kia Center
moments.why: The weekly civic ritual where all of these communities share a room.

vocabulary.meaning: Local nickname for Orlando, used affectionately by natives and transplants.
The area code and civic badge, with 321 and 689 overlays for the wider region.
Orlando's official-feeling nickname, tied to lakes, parks and the downtown fountain.
Puerto Rican identity term, used proudly across Central Florida.
Disney's term for employees, used by locals who work in the parks.
A Publix deli sub, a Florida staple and a shared local ritual.
Local shorthand for the Mills 50 district.

designCues.cue: Magic blue and silver with black pinstripe heritage
designCues.source: The Magic's long-standing primary color and pinstripe uniform legacy.
designCues.use: Anchor every Orlando collection with it, and add black and silver pinstripes on warm-ups and jerseys.

designCues.source: Central Florida's citrus heritage and the Orange County name.
designCues.use: Use it as an accent or sunset-faded gradient, not a main color, so it doesn't clash with team marks.

designCues.cue: Lake Eola swan and fountain line art
designCues.source: Downtown's best-known landmark that isn't a theme park.
designCues.use: Simplify it into a one-weight line drawing for tees and caps, commissioned from a local illustrator.

designCues.source: Hand-painted signage and neon on the Mills 50 corridor.
designCues.use: Build a custom wordmark style on commissioned local lettering, and credit the letterer.

designCues.source: Daily summer storm skies over Orlando's lakes.
designCues.use: Run it as a gradient on dye-wash shirts and outerwear, with orange accents.

designCues.source: The heat and humidity that dominate the local wardrobe.
designCues.use: Put vented mesh and light woven textures on shooting shirts and warm-up layers.
Use bold numerals as a sleeve or hem graphic, in Magic colors.

designCues.source: Puerto Rican identity in east Orlando and Kissimmee.
designCues.use: Make it only through a paid, credited collaboration with Central Florida Puerto Rican artists.

productHooks: Heritage pinstripe capsule honoring the Shaq and Penny era, with Hardaway-linked footwear and warm-ups timed to the opening weeks.
A 407 Day drop for April: numeral graphics, citrus-and-blue colors, lightweight tees and shorts.
Boricua-rooted Hispanic Heritage Month capsule, co-created with Central Florida Puerto Rican artists and launching around mid-October.
Heat-and-storm collection: vented shooting shirts, packable rain shells and quick-dry shorts in lake-twilight gradients.
watchouts: Never commercialize the Pulse tragedy or its memorial imagery. Partner with community organizations on any Pride product.
Avoid Disney, Universal and other theme-park IP and imagery. It's licensed, and it isn't how locals see themselves.
Puerto Rican, Black and Vietnamese cues must come from paid, credited local creators. Don't lift symbols.
Magic wordmarks and legacy logos need NBA and team licensing. Player likenesses need separate clearance.
